title: Where the sun sets
hook: your sunset point slides along the horizon through the year

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sandhya, the joining, the seam between parts of the day, especially dusk. Your line was watch it go.

Where, exactly, does the sun set from your home? Behind which building, which tree, which hill? "In the west" is the usual answer. True, roughly. But watch from the same spot every evening for a year, and you'd see what the builders of Stonehenge tracked with care. The sunset point doesn't stay put. It walks, slowly, all year, back and forth along the horizon.
screen: `BEHIND WHICH TREE?` → `NOT THE SAME PLACE TWICE.` → `WHERE THE SUN SETS.`

segments.voice: The Earth is tilted, a bit more than twenty-three degrees, and as it circles the sun, that tilt shifts the sun's path across our sky through the year. On two days, the equinoxes in March and September, the sun sets almost exactly due west. After the March equinox, in the northern half of the world, the sunset point creeps north, day after day, to its farthest point at the June solstice. There it seems to pause, then turns back south, passing west again in September, all the way to its southern limit at the December solstice. In the southern half of the world, it's the mirror image. At the latitude of New York or Madrid, the whole swing is wide, roughly sixty degrees of horizon. Solstice comes from Latin words meaning the sun stands still, because at the turning points it seems to linger for a few days before heading back. People have watched this for thousands of years, with great care. Stonehenge, in England, is lined up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset. And in New York City, twice a year, the setting sun lines up exactly with the cross streets, flooding them with light, and crowds gather to watch; the astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson gave it the name Manhattanhenge. There's something steadying in it. The sunset point is always moving, and always coming back: change and return, in one slow sweep.
screen: `THE TILT OF THE EARTH.` · `DUE WEST AT THE EQUINOXES.` · `SOLSTICE: THE SUN STANDS STILL.` · `STONEHENGE TO MANHATTANHENGE.` · then, large: `IT MOVES.`

segments.voice: Picture the place you watched from yesterday, or a window facing roughly west, and the horizon there: a roofline, a tree, a pole, a hill. Pick one landmark, the one the sun will go down against tonight, and the spot you could look again from in a few weeks. For now, just picture the slow walk of the light.
Solstice, from Latin words meaning the sun stands still, the point where the sunset's yearly swing turns back. Today's word.
Your line: it moves. One landmark is enough to see it. That's day one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Sky watchers, farmers and photographers track where the sun sets against a fixed landmark through the year, and some ancient monuments, like Stonehenge, are aligned with solstice sunrises and sunsets.
